overview: This file consists of thirty consecutive “List of Papers” register sheets—internally numbered 31–60—indexing State Department correspondence concerning petroleum in Japan from December 1934 through October 1939. The entries document American and British oil companies’ difficulties under Japan’s Petroleum Industry Law, particularly compulsory stockholding, import and sales quotas, refining permits, and government control of distribution; they also trace coordinated diplomatic representations by the United States and Britain, negotiations involving Standard-Vacuum, Shell/Rising Sun, Mitsui, and Japanese officials, and related developments in Korea, Manchuria, Mexico, Colombia, synthetic fuels, hydrogenation, and Japan’s search for secure wartime oil supplies. The sheets summarize telegrams, despatches, memoranda, letters, press clippings, acknowledgments, and cross-references rather than reproducing the underlying documents.

subfiles.title: List of Papers register for Petroleum—Japan, entries 164–339
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State file staff
subfiles.about: A chronological register summarizes and cross-references State Department papers concerning petroleum regulation, foreign oil interests, and Japanese efforts to secure oil supplies between 1934 and 1939.
subfiles.summary: The register traces the prolonged dispute over Japan’s Petroleum Industry Law, especially its six-month stockholding requirement, quotas, refining permissions, and the security of Standard-Vacuum and Shell operations. It records negotiations with Kurusu, Yoshino, Hirota, Matsushima, Mitsui representatives, and other Japanese officials, alongside coordinated American and British diplomatic representations. Later entries broaden the subject to Korean quotas, Manchurian policy, hydrogenation and synthetic petroleum, Japanese petroleum initiatives in Mexico and Colombia, refinery construction, and increasingly comprehensive government control of petroleum distribution. Numerous entries are cross-reference notices directing readers to related State Department decimal files rather than complete documents reproduced here.

interest: The register is especially useful as a detailed chronological roadmap to a dispersed body of diplomatic and corporate records, showing almost day-by-day interaction among the State Department, the American and British embassies, private oil firms, and Japanese ministries. It reveals how a nominally commercial dispute over storage and quotas became entangled with diplomacy, strategic dependence on imported oil, preparations for military contingencies, and Japan’s search for alternative supplies and synthetic-fuel technology. The entries also identify many conversations, enclosures, press reports, and cross-file references that could guide a historian to underlying documents not present in this OCR. Because these pages are an administrative index rather than the original correspondence, heavily corrupted names and locations—particularly in the Colombia-related entry—should be checked against the scans or referenced papers before quotation.
